name: sqlite3
one_line: Open a SQLite database file and run SQL on it: list tables, read rows, search, count.
plain: Open a SQLite database file and run SQL on it: list tables, read rows, search, count.
The sections below show when to use it, real examples, and the options explained in plain English.
when: Browser history, app data and many forensics challenges ship as `.db`/`.sqlite` files.

examples.title: Create a small database
examples.cmd: rm -f t.db; sqlite3 t.db "CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER, name TEXT, role TEXT); INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'alice','user'),(2,'bob','admin'),(3,'carol','user');" && sqlite3 t.db '.tables'

examples.title: Read it nicely
examples.output: (expected, not captured) A header row id name role, a dashed line, then three rows.

examples.title: Filter and count
examples.cmd: sqlite3 -header -column t.db "SELECT role, COUNT(*) AS n FROM users GROUP BY role;"

examples.title: Look at the structure
examples.output: (expected, not captured) CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER, name TEXT, role TEXT);

options.use: Find a user, URL or message

options.flag: ORDER BY / LIMIT / GROUP BY / COUNT(*)

options.plain: Print the whole database as SQL

mistakes: Dot-commands (`.tables`) are sqlite3 features, not SQL; they take no semicolon.
Open evidence with `-readonly` or a copy.
SQLite types are loose: text may hide in number columns.
Browser databases may be locked while the browser runs: copy the file first.
try: List the tables of a browser history database copy.
Find the most visited domain with `GROUP BY`.
see_also: MySQL client, DB Browser for SQLite, python sqlite3 module, strings, grep.
